title: Kashmiri Pandits mark 36th Balidan Diwas, demand genocide recognition and homeland
excerpt: Displaced Kashmiri Pandits observed the 36th Balidan Diwas in Jammu on September 14, renewing long-standing demands for a genocide law and a separate homeland in the Valley under direct Union protection.
body:
• Displaced Kashmiri Pandits observed the 36th Balidan Diwas in Jammu on September 14, honouring community members and security personnel killed in violence in Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Panun Kashmir, which organised the event, renewed its demands for a law recognising the community's suffering as "genocide" and a separate homeland in the Valley under direct Union protection.
  • Community leaders raised alarms over the safety of Kashmiri Pandit employees working in the Valley under the Prime Minister's employment package, describing them as effectively "hostages".
  • The Jammu State People's Movement linked the Pandits' homeland demand with Jammu's own demand for statehood, arguing the two causes strengthen each other.

Displaced Kashmiri Pandits on Monday observed the 36th 'Balidan Diwas' in Jammu, paying homage to members of the community and security personnel who lost their lives to violence and terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir. Participants at the programme organised by Panun Kashmir wore black armbands as a mark of remembrance, and a "Veer Jyoti" dedicated to the dead was lit before being carried to the Bhadrakali Temple at Thalwal on the outskirts of Jammu, where it was installed as the "Amar Jyoti", according to The Hindu.

Context & Background

September 14 holds particular significance for the community. It marks the killing of Kashmiri Pandit leader Tika Lal Taploo in the Valley in September 1989 — an assassination community leaders describe as the beginning of the violence that drove Kashmiri Pandits from their homes. The community has observed the day since 1990, following the mass migration from the Valley in early 1990.

https://x.com/GreaterKashmir/status/2099450516636074465

Panun Kashmir, a representative body of migrant Kashmiri Hindus, traces its political demand to the Margdarshan Resolution adopted by the community after the exodus. Its chairman, Tito Ganju, told PTI that the day honours both those killed by terrorism after 1990 and those the community believes suffered through what it describes as seven waves of persecution over the past 700 years.

"We have been observing this day since 1990 to honour the martyrs and reaffirm our commitment to continue the struggle till the achievement of our goal, which is the enactment of a genocide bill and a separate homeland as enshrined in the Margdarshan Resolution."

— Tito Ganju, Chairman, Panun Kashmir

Impact & Analysis

The centrepiece of this year's observance was a renewed push for statutory recognition. Panun Kashmir proposed a genocide bill in 2020, and Ganju argued that without legal recognition the community's suffering remains a matter of "narrative interpretation" rather than acknowledgement of a crime of the "highest legal order". The absence of such a law, he said, has produced a lack of accountability and no guarantees against recurrence. He framed the struggle in constitutional terms, citing the rights guaranteed under Articles 14, 19 and 21, which he said had seen "gross violation" for 36 years.

The homeland demand was equally firm. Panun Kashmir wants a reorganised Jammu and Kashmir with a separate homeland for displaced Kashmiri Hindus where legislative and executive control rests with "pro-India elements". Ganju was blunt: "Without a separate homeland, we believe there is no other way forward."

Security concerns for Kashmiri Pandit employees working in the Valley under the Prime Minister's employment package formed a third strand. Ganju said recent threats showed that despite an overall improvement in the situation, rehabilitation would not succeed without a fundamental change in the security environment. "Our children who are there are effectively hostages," he said.

Local political backing came from Col (Retd) Ajay Raina, chairman of the Jammu State People's Movement, who linked the Pandits' demand for a separate homeland with Jammu's demand for statehood: "neither side can truly move forward without the other." A separate function at the Jiya-pota Ghat in Akhnoor, reported by Scoop News, saw floral tributes at the martyrs' memorial on the banks of the Chenab, where Panun Kashmir leaders recalled the exodus and the sacrifices that followed.

Diaspora Angle

The Kashmiri Pandit diaspora — including organisations such as the Kashmiri Overseas Association in the US and the Global Kashmiri Pandit Diaspora — has kept the community's political demands alive internationally. Earlier this year, seven community organisations announced a Global Kashmiri Pandit Conclave, drawing delegates from India, the United States, Europe and the Middle East, with heritage preservation and the question of return on the agenda.

What's Next

Panun Kashmir shows no sign of moderating its twin demands: the genocide bill and the separate homeland. The organisation also wants an employment package for 15,000 displaced youth and an increase in the monthly cash relief paid to the community, according to the Early Times. "Struggle is the only option we have," Ganju said. "If we had not struggled, this chapter would have been closed long back."
